title: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
summary: How an LLM server schedules every iteration with continuous batching, accounts for KV cache memory, avoids fragmentation with block tables, and decides when to admit, preempt, swap or recompute.
outcomes: Explain the roles of the scheduler, KV cache manager and model executor in one engine step
Explain why iteration-level scheduling with selective batching beats request-level batching
Compute KV bytes per token, KV pool size and how many sequences fit for a real model
Compare contiguous and paged KV allocation in terms of reserved, internal and external waste
Choose between reservation, preemption, swapping and recomputation for a given workload

lessons.title: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time

blocks.md:
Your GPT can generate text with a `for` loop: run the model, sample a token, append it, repeat. A serving system faces a harder problem. Thousands of requests arrive at random times, each with a different prompt length and an output length nobody knows in advance, and all of them must share one GPU's memory.

Recall from the GPU course: **prefill** runs the whole prompt through the model in one compute-bound pass, **decode** then produces one token per pass and is limited by memory bandwidth, and batching many sequences shares each weight read. This course is about the software that decides, every few milliseconds, which sequences form that batch and where their memory lives.

Both papers this course leans on split the server the same way. Orca (Yu et al., OSDI 2022) has a **request pool**, a **scheduler** and an **execution engine**. vLLM (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023) has a **centralized scheduler**, a **KV cache manager** and **GPU workers**.

- The **scheduler** picks which requests run in the next step and how many of their tokens.
- The **KV cache manager** owns the GPU memory that holds every request's keys and values (the *KV cache*) and says yes or no to each allocation.
- The **model executor** (workers, one per GPU) runs the forward pass. It does not make policy decisions.

blocks.title: One request through one engine step

nodes.label:
KV cache manager
block pool, tables

scenes.caption: A prompt arrives over HTTP. The API server turns text into token ids; it never touches the GPU.
The request joins the scheduler's waiting queue. Nothing runs yet: the scheduler admits work only at step boundaries.
Before admitting it, the scheduler asks the KV cache manager whether enough free blocks exist for the prompt's keys and values. If not, the request keeps waiting.
The scheduler sends one control message per step: the token ids to process for every scheduled request plus each request's block table.
The workers run one forward pass for the whole batch. Attention reads earlier tokens' K and V from the blocks named in the tables and writes the new ones.
Each request's sampled token comes back to the scheduler, which appends it, checks stop conditions and hands text to the API server to stream.
When the request stops, the scheduler tells the KV cache manager to free its blocks, and the next step can admit someone else into that memory.

blocks.md:
The heart of the server is a loop the papers call an **iteration** or **step**: schedule, run one forward pass, process outputs, repeat. Orca's scheduler does exactly this: select requests, invoke the engine for one iteration, receive the generated tokens. vLLM's current architecture runs the scheduler and KV cache manager inside an **engine core** process with a busy loop, a separate **API server** process for HTTP and tokenization, and one **GPU worker** process per GPU.

Two latency numbers come out of this loop. **Time to first token (TTFT)** covers queueing plus the prefill step. **Inter-token latency (ITL)**, also called time per output token, is the gap between later tokens, roughly the duration of one step. Throughput is the total tokens produced per second across all requests.

Tensor parallelism splits each layer's attention heads across GPUs. Every shard still processes the same token positions, so the vLLM paper keeps a *single* KV cache manager in the scheduler: all workers use the same physical block ids, and each worker stores only the slice of K and V for its own heads. Per step, the scheduler broadcasts token ids and block tables; the workers synchronize activations among themselves with all-reduce and send sampled tokens back. The workers never negotiate memory with each other.

The scheduler decides **what** runs each step, the KV cache manager decides whether it **fits**, and the executor just runs a forward pass over token ids and block tables. Almost every serving optimization in this course is a change to the first two.

blocks.question: A model runs with tensor parallelism over 4 GPUs. Why can one KV cache manager in the scheduler hand the same block table to all 4 workers?
options: Each worker stores the whole KV cache, so memory is simply replicated 4 times
Every shard processes the same token positions and stores only its own heads' slice, so block ids mean the same thing on every GPU
Workers allocate blocks themselves and report back after every step
Block tables are only used on GPU 0, which forwards keys and values to the others
blocks.explain: Tensor parallelism splits heads, not positions. Block 17 holds positions 32 to 47 on every GPU, each GPU keeping the K and V of its own heads there. One mapping therefore serves all workers, which is why vLLM centralizes the manager.

blocks.question: A server is busy decoding 200 requests when a new request with a 3,000-token prompt arrives. Which latency number is this new request's prefill step most directly part of?
options: Its time to first token
Its inter-token latency
The throughput of the other requests only
None, prefill happens before the request is queued
blocks.explain: The first token can only be sampled after the prompt's keys and values exist, so queueing plus the prefill step make up TTFT. That same step can also slow the 200 running requests' next token, which is the tension the next lesson's token budget manages.

blocks.md:
Classic model servers schedule at **request granularity**: form a batch, run it until every request in it is done, then form the next one. Orca's paper names the two failures this causes for text generation. **Early-finished** requests keep occupying the batch (the engine even keeps computing for them) and cannot be returned until the slowest request ends. **Late-joining** requests must wait for the whole running batch to finish before they can start.

The GPU course showed the resulting timeline. Here we look at what a scheduler must do differently to fix it.

Orca's answer is **iteration-level scheduling**: the scheduler regains control after *every* forward pass. It repeats three things: select the requests to run next, invoke the engine for one iteration over them, and receive one output token per request. A finished request is returned at once, and a new request waits at most one iteration before it can be picked. This is what other systems call **continuous batching** or **in-flight batching** (TensorRT-LLM's term).

There is a catch. In one iteration some requests are decoding a single token while new ones are prefilling prompts of different lengths, so their inputs cannot be stacked into one rectangular `[B, L, H]` tensor (B requests, L tokens each, hidden size H). Orca's fix is **selective batching**: flatten all tokens of all requests into one `[sum of L, H]` matrix for the operations that do not care which request a token belongs to, and split by request only for attention.

blocks.title: Selective batching in Orca (one layer, simplified)

scenes.caption: Orca's example batch: x1 and x2 are decoding (1 new token each), x3 and x4 are new prompts with 2 and 3 tokens. Padding them into one [B, L, H] tensor is impossible, so all 7 tokens are flattened into [7, H].
Linear layers, LayerNorm, GeLU and residual adds treat every token independently, so they run once over the 7-row matrix. This is where batching pays: one weight read serves all 7 tokens.
Attention must only mix tokens of the same request, so a Split operation cuts the 7 rows back into per-request pieces.
Decoding requests also need keys and values of all their earlier tokens, which the K/V manager kept from previous iterations. Prompts attend among their own new tokens.
Merge stacks the outputs back into [7, H] and the following linear layers are batched again. The engine returns one sampled token per request.

blocks.tex: X \in \mathbb{R}^{\left(\sum_{i} L_i\right) \times H},\qquad L_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{request } i \text{ decoding} \\ \text{prompt length} & \text{request } i \text{ prefilling} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: The packed input of one step. Matrix multiplies and norms run over all rows at once; only attention needs the per-request boundaries.

blocks.md: Modern engines keep this design and make the step size explicit as a **token budget**. vLLM's current scheduler treats prompt and output tokens the same way: each step it builds a map from request id to number of tokens to compute, bounded by `max_num_batched_tokens` (tokens per step) and `max_num_seqs` (requests per step). With **chunked prefill**, enabled by default where possible, it schedules running requests first, so pending decodes always get their token, then fills the leftover budget with prefills, cutting a prompt into chunks if it does not fit. TensorRT-LLM exposes the same two limits as `max_batch_size` and `max_num_tokens`.

blocks.prompt: Budget 12 tokens, at most 4 requests. R1 and R2 arrive with 5-token prompts, R3 with a 7-token prompt. After R1 and R2 prefill in step 1, only 2 tokens of budget remain. What should happen to R3 in step 1?
blocks.reveal: Without chunking, R3 simply cannot run: 7 tokens do not fit in 2, so it waits a full step (TensorRT-LLM's documentation shows exactly this situation). With **chunked prefill**, R3 runs its first 2 prompt tokens now and the remaining 5 next step. Its KV cache for positions 0 and 1 is written in step 1 and reused in step 2, just like a decode reuses earlier tokens.

blocks.title: Packing a 12-token budget, at most 4 requests

scenes.caption: Step 1: R1 and R2 each prefill 5 prompt tokens. Only 2 tokens of budget remain, so the 7-token prompt of R3 is chunked: its first 2 tokens run now.
Step 2: running requests go first. R1 and R2 decode 1 token each, R3 finishes its last 5 prompt tokens, and R4's 4-token prompt fits. R5 waits: 4 requests is the sequence limit.
Step 3: four decodes use only 4 of 12 tokens. The budget is not the limit here, the sequence cap is. R1 emits its 3rd and last token and finishes.
Step 4: R1's slot was freed at the end of step 3, so R5's 9-token prompt joins the same step as three decodes: 12 tokens, a full budget.
Step 5: R2 and R3 finish. Requests left and joined at step boundaries, never waiting for a whole batch to drain.

blocks.md: The budget is a latency dial. vLLM's tuning guide says a smaller `max_num_batched_tokens` (for example 2048) gives better inter-token latency because fewer prefill tokens slow down each decode step, while a larger budget gives better time to first token because more prompt tokens are processed per step. Mixing the two kinds of work in one step also helps utilization: prefill tokens are compute-bound, decode tokens are memory-bound, so they use different resources of the same GPU pass.

Continuous batching does **not** mean padding requests to a common length. The tokens are packed with no padding, and only attention looks at per-request boundaries. TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching explicitly requires packed (unpadded) inputs for this reason.
The scheduler's unit of work is a step with a token budget, not a request. Requests enter and leave between steps, and every step is a fresh decision about who gets how many tokens.

blocks.question: Budget 2048 tokens per step, chunked prefill on. 50 requests are decoding when a 6,000-token prompt arrives. What happens over the next few steps?
options: The 50 decodes pause until the 6,000-token prefill finishes in one large step
The prompt is rejected because it exceeds the token budget
Each step runs the 50 decode tokens first and spends the remaining 1,998 tokens on the next chunk of the prompt, so the prefill takes about 4 steps while decoding never stops
The prompt is split across 50 requests, one chunk each
blocks.explain: Decodes are scheduled first (1 token each), and the leftover budget goes to prefill chunks: 6,000 / 1,998 is a bit over 3, so 4 steps. Inter-token latency of the 50 stays bounded, and the new request's TTFT grows a little in exchange.

blocks.question: Why does selective batching split the batch for attention but not for the QKV projection?
options: Attention has no weights, so batching it gains nothing and it must be skipped
The QKV projection runs on the CPU
Splitting the projection would require padding, splitting attention does not
Each token's projection uses only that token's row, but attention must combine a token only with earlier tokens of its own request
blocks.explain: A linear layer computes each output row from one input row, so the request a row belongs to is irrelevant and all rows share one weight read. Attention mixes rows, and mixing rows from different requests would be wrong, so it needs the boundaries (and each request's own past keys and values).

lessons.title: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size

blocks.md: Every serving decision in the last lesson silently assumed the answer to one question: does this request's KV cache fit? To answer it the scheduler needs exact accounting. Each layer stores one key vector and one value vector per **KV head** for every token. With **grouped-query attention (GQA)**, several query heads share one KV head, so the number of KV heads $n_{kv}$ can be much smaller than the number of query heads.

blocks.tex: \text{bytes per token} = 2 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{kv} \times d_{\text{head}} \times b
blocks.caption: 2 for K and V; b is bytes per value (2 for FP16 or BF16, 1 for FP8).

blocks.md:
Worked example: **Llama 3 8B**. The Llama 3 paper lists 32 layers, model dimension 4,096, 32 attention heads and 8 key/value heads, so $d_{\text{head}} = 4096/32 = 128$. In BF16:

$2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072$ bytes, exactly **128 KiB per token**.

The GPU course found 512 KiB per token for LLaMA-7B, which has a similar size but one KV head per query head. GQA with 8 KV heads cuts this by 4x. A full 8,192-token context still costs $8192 \times 128$ KiB $= 1$ GiB, and Llama 3 70B (80 layers, also 8 KV heads) needs 320 KiB per token.

Next, how much memory is there for KV? Engines decide this once at startup. vLLM's `gpu_memory_utilization` is the fraction of GPU memory the engine may use; it loads the weights, runs a profiling pass with dummy inputs to measure peak activation memory, and turns the rest into KV blocks. TensorRT-LLM's `free_gpu_memory_fraction` (default 0.9) is the share of *free* GPU memory given to the KV cache. Worked numbers below assume an 80 GB GPU (80 x 10^9 bytes), a 0.9 fraction of the whole GPU, and 4 GB of activations.

blocks.title: How an 80 GB GPU is carved up at startup (Llama 3 8B)

scenes.caption: The engine may use 90% of 80 GB, so 8 GB is left alone. Loading 8 billion BF16 parameters takes 16 GB.
A profiling forward pass with dummy inputs measures peak activation and workspace memory. We assume 4 GB here; the real figure depends on the token budget.
Everything left becomes one pool of KV blocks, allocated once up front: 52 GB. This number, not compute, will cap how many requests can run.

blocks.caption: The pool for our example, in tokens and in 16-token blocks (vLLM's default block size).

blocks.md: Now the batch size. If each request reserves its full 8,192-token context, only $\lfloor 396{,}728 / 8192 \rfloor = 48$ requests fit, no matter how short they turn out to be. If each request holds only the blocks it actually uses, a 1,500-token sequence needs $\lceil 1500/16 \rceil = 94$ blocks (1,504 slots) and $\lfloor 24{,}795 / 94 \rfloor = 263$ of them fit. That is 5.5x more sequences to share each weight read, from bookkeeping alone.

blocks.title: How many sequences fit in the KV pool

scenes.caption: Llama 3 8B, 128 KiB per token, 52 GB pool. Reserving the full 8,192-token context per request caps the batch at 48. Allocating only what is used fits 263 sequences of 1,500 tokens.
Same pool with 512 KiB per token (a model with full multi-head attention, like LLaMA-7B). Every curve drops 4x: GQA's smaller KV directly multiplies the batch size.
An FP8 KV cache stores 1 byte per value, halving the per-token size to 64 KiB, so twice as many sequences fit at every length.
Shrinking the pool to 20 GB (say, a bigger model on the same GPU) scales every curve down proportionally. Both knobs act the same way: capacity is pool size divided by bytes per token.

blocks.md: Model weights are paid once; KV is paid per token per sequence. A common mistake is to size a deployment by "the model fits on the GPU". A model that fits with 2 GB to spare can serve almost nobody: 2 GB is only about 15,000 tokens of Llama 3 8B's KV cache.

Capacity in sequences is roughly pool bytes / (bytes per token x tokens per sequence). Every lever (GQA, FP8 KV, more GPUs, smaller weights, shorter contexts, less waste per sequence) moves one of those three terms.

blocks.question: Llama 3 70B has 80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads and head dimension 128. What is its BF16 KV cache per token?
options: 160 KiB
2.5 MiB
320 KiB
640 KiB
blocks.explain: 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 327,680 bytes = 320 KiB. Using the 64 query heads instead of the 8 KV heads gives 2.5 MiB (the GQA mistake); dropping the factor 2 for K and V gives 160 KiB; using 4-byte values gives 640 KiB.

blocks.question: All requests are about 2,000 tokens long and memory-bound by KV. Which single change roughly doubles the number of sequences that fit?
options: Storing the KV cache in FP8 instead of BF16
Doubling max_num_seqs
Doubling the block size from 16 to 32
Enabling chunked prefill
blocks.explain: FP8 halves b in the formula, so twice as many tokens fit in the same pool. Raising max_num_seqs only lifts a cap that is not binding; block size changes waste per sequence by a few tokens; chunked prefill changes step composition, not memory per token.

lessons.title: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables

blocks.md:
Why did older servers reserve the maximum length? Most deep learning frameworks want each tensor in one contiguous piece of memory, so systems like FasterTransformer and Orca stored each request's KV cache as one contiguous chunk sized for the longest output it might produce. The vLLM paper names three resulting kinds of waste:

- **Reserved**: slots that will hold this request's future tokens, but sit empty for most of its life.
- **Internal fragmentation**: slots past the point where the request actually stopped, never used.
- **External fragmentation**: free memory between chunks that is too small for the next request.

It measured only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV memory holding real token states in those systems.

To see the mechanism with numbers you can trace, the bars below come from a toy simulation (script-computed, not from a paper). Pool: 65,536 token slots, which is 8 GiB at Llama 3 8B's 128 KiB per token. Workload: 20,000 queued requests with prompts of 64 to 1,024 tokens, a client-set maximum length of 512, 1,024 or 2,048 tokens, and exponentially distributed outputs averaging 300 tokens before the cap. One token per running request per step, 4,000 steps, measured after a 500-step warmup.

blocks.title: Where the KV pool goes: toy simulation, 8 GiB pool

scenes.caption: Contiguous, first-fit, each request reserves its client-set maximum length (512, 1024 or 2048). Only 41% of the pool holds real tokens; a third is never-to-be-used tail space.
Paged, block size 16, blocks allocated when needed. 98.4% holds real tokens. Nothing is reserved ahead, and the only internal waste is the unfilled tail of each sequence's last block (1.1%).
Paged with block size 128. Same scheme, but each last block wastes up to 127 slots, so internal fragmentation grows to 8.2% and real tokens fall to 91.3%.

blocks.md: Paging fixes all three wastes at once, the same way an operating system does. Memory is cut into equal **physical blocks** (vLLM's default is 16 tokens). A request owns a list of **logical blocks** filled left to right, and its **block table** maps each logical block to whichever physical block it got. A new block is allocated only when the last one is full, so nothing is reserved ahead, internal waste is at most one partly filled block per sequence (about $B/2$ tokens on average), and since every block is the same size, any free block fits any request: no external fragmentation.

blocks.title: Virtual memory concepts, mapped to the KV cache

scenes.caption: The vLLM paper's analogy: a request is a process and its tokens are the bytes of its address space.
The KV cache is split into fixed-size blocks, like pages. Logical blocks are filled left to right as tokens arrive.
Each request has a block table mapping logical to physical blocks. There is no MMU or TLB: the attention kernel reads the table itself and computes addresses in software.
Physical blocks are interchangeable, so any free block can back any logical block. Equal sizes mean no external fragmentation.
When memory runs out, an OS swaps pages to disk. The KV manager can swap blocks to CPU memory, or throw them away and recompute them, an option an OS does not have.

blocks.md: For the scheduler, paging turns memory accounting into integer arithmetic. Instead of searching for a large enough hole, "does it fit?" becomes "is the number of blocks this request needs at most the number of free blocks?".

blocks.title: The manager's view: block tables and a free count (block size 4)

scenes.caption: Prefill: A (6-token prompt) gets blocks 0 and 1; B (3 tokens) gets block 2. The manager only needs a count of free blocks to admit them: 5 left.
Two decode steps later A holds 8 tokens (block 1 now full) and B holds 5, so B's 5th token needed a new block: block 3. Free count 4.

C arrives with a 9-token prompt, needing ceil(9/4) = 3 blocks. 3 is at most 4, so it is admitted into blocks 4, 5, 6. Admission needed only a count of free blocks, not a search for a large enough hole.

A's 9th token crosses a block boundary and takes the last free block, 7, so A's blocks 0, 1, 7 are no longer contiguous, which is fine. The pool is now full; the next block request will need a policy (next lesson).
B finishes. Its blocks 2 and 3 return to the free pool immediately and can be reused by anyone, in any order. No compaction, no searching for a large enough hole.

blocks.md: The analogy is not exact, and the differences matter. The OS translates every memory access in hardware; here the attention kernel is rewritten to fetch keys and values block by block through the table (the PagedAttention course covers that kernel, block sharing and prefix caching in depth). An OS evicts individual pages by predicted reuse; a sequence needs *all* its blocks every step, so vLLM evicts all or nothing per sequence. And an OS cannot recreate a page it threw away, while a KV block can always be recomputed from the tokens.

Paging does not shrink the KV cache. A 1,500-token sequence still needs 1,500 tokens of K and V. Paging removes the memory that held *nothing*, which is why the gain is largest when requests are short relative to their maximum length.
Fixed-size blocks plus a per-request table make KV memory behave like virtual memory: allocate on demand, any block fits anywhere, and waste is bounded by one partial block per sequence.

blocks.question: In the contiguous simulation, 12.8% of the pool was free yet the next request in line could not start. Which kind of waste is this?
options: Internal fragmentation
Reserved slots
Activation memory
External fragmentation
blocks.explain: Free memory existed, but not as one contiguous run long enough for the waiting request's reservation. That is external fragmentation. With fixed-size blocks any free block is usable, so external fragmentation disappears; the 0.5% left free in the paged run is just too few blocks for the next prompt.

blocks.question: Paging lets a server admit a request after allocating only its prompt's blocks. What new problem does this create that max-length reservation did not have?
options: Requests can no longer share a batch
The pool can run out in the middle of generation, when running requests need new blocks that are not there
Prompts longer than one block cannot be stored
Block tables use more memory than the KV cache itself
blocks.explain: Reservation guaranteed every admitted request could finish. Allocating on demand bets that not everyone will grow at once; when the bet loses, some running request has nowhere to put its next token. Handling that is the job of preemption, the next lesson.

lessons.title: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption

blocks.md: A KV cache only grows, and nobody knows how long any request will run. Every scheduler therefore needs a rule for **admission control** (when to start a new request) and, unless that rule is very cautious, a rule for **preemption** (what to do when running requests outgrow memory).

Orca chose caution. When a request is scheduled for the first time, the scheduler reserves its `max_tokens` (the most tokens it can ever have) out of `n_slots`, the total number of KV slots the operator configured. If the reservation does not fit, the request waits. The paper explains why: without it, the scheduler can deadlock, unable to run any request because there is no room for anyone's next key and value.

blocks.caption: The admission part of Orca's Algorithm 1, rewritten in Python. A request's slots are released when it finishes.

blocks.md: vLLM bets the other way: allocate blocks only as tokens arrive, and handle the rare case when the pool runs out. Its paper fixes three rules. Scheduling is **first come, first served**, and when it must preempt it evicts the **latest arrivals first**, so early requests are not starved. Eviction is **all or nothing** per sequence, because a sequence needs all of its blocks every step. And sequences of one request (say, beam candidates) are **gang-scheduled**: preempted and resumed together. The paper also says that while preempted sequences are pending, no new requests are accepted.

blocks.title: A preemption step (simplified from vLLM's scheduler)
blocks.code:
def schedule(running, waiting, pool):
    preempted = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(running):              # oldest request first
        req = running[i]
        need = pool.blocks_needed(req)   # 0 or 1 block this step
        while need > pool.num_free and running[-1] is not req:
            victim = running.pop()       # latest arrival loses
            pool.free_all(victim)        # all or nothing
            victim.num_computed = 0      # its KV will be recomputed
            waiting.appendleft(victim)   # first in line to resume
            preempted.append(victim.id)
        if need > pool.num_free:         # nobody left to evict
            running.pop(i); pool.free_all(req)
            req.num_computed = 0
            waiting.appendleft(req); preempted.append(req.id)
            break
        pool.allocate(req, need)
        i += 1
    if not preempted:
        admit(waiting, running, pool)    # FCFS while blocks remain
    return preempted

scenes.caption: Running requests in arrival order: A, B, C. One free block. A's next token crosses a block boundary, so it needs 1 block.
A fits: it takes the last free block.
B also crosses a boundary and needs 1 block, but none are free.
The latest arrival, C, is the victim. All 3 of its blocks are freed at once, and its progress counter is reset because its KV is gone.
C goes to the front of the waiting queue, so it is the first to resume when memory frees up.
B now gets its block. The loop ends: A and B both decode this step.
A preemption happened, so no new request is admitted this step even though 2 blocks are free. Admitting one now would only invite the next preemption.
scenes.output:
preempted: ['C']
C later re-runs its prompt plus already generated tokens as one prefill.

blocks.md:
What happens to an evicted sequence's KV? The vLLM paper offers two recovery methods.

- **Swapping**: copy the blocks to CPU memory, managed by a separate CPU block allocator, and copy them back on resume. Swap space never needs to exceed the GPU's KV pool.
- **Recomputation**: drop the blocks. On resume, the prompt plus the tokens already generated become one longer prompt, rebuilt in a single prefill step, which is much faster than regenerating them one by one.

Its ablation found that swapping suffers with small blocks, because many small CPU-GPU transfers waste bandwidth, while recompute cost does not depend on block size. Recompute wins with small blocks, swap with large ones, and for 16 to 64 they performed comparably.

blocks.title: Restoring a preempted sequence: a first-order cost model

scenes.caption: Llama 3 8B, 20 GB/s effective transfer, 200 TFLOP/s effective compute. Swapping moves 256 KiB per token (out and back) in about 13 us; recomputing costs 2N FLOPs per token, about 80 us. Swap looks cheaper here.
Small blocks mean many small copies, and the vLLM paper found these cannot use the link's full bandwidth. At 3 GB/s effective, swap costs more than recompute.
A 13B model with full multi-head attention stores 800 KiB per token. Both costs rise, and at 20 GB/s swap is still cheaper on paper: the answer depends on the model's KV size per FLOP.

blocks.md: Current vLLM makes the choice for you: its docs say that in V1 the default preemption mode is recompute, because recomputation has lower overhead in that architecture, and CPU swapping for preemption has been removed. If preemption happens often, the docs recommend more KV memory (`gpu_memory_utilization`, more tensor or pipeline parallelism) or fewer concurrent tokens (`max_num_seqs`, `max_num_batched_tokens`).

The other engines sit between the two extremes. **TensorRT-LLM** makes it a setting: its default capacity policy `GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT` admits a request only if the blocks it needs *to completion* can be reserved, so a started request is never paused. `MAX_UTILIZATION` packs as many requests as possible and may pause some when KV runs out. **SGLang** estimates instead of reserving every worst case: a new request is budgeted for its prompt plus its `max_new_tokens` (clipped at 4,096), but requests already running count only their remaining `max_new_tokens` times a *new token ratio*. The ratio starts at a cautious 0.7 and decays every decode step toward a much smaller floor, so admission grows more optimistic over time. When decoding runs out of memory, it **retracts** some running requests back to the queue and resets the ratio from how much the remaining requests have actually generated.

blocks.title: Admission policy vs outcome (same toy simulation)

scenes.caption: Average number of running sequences. Reserving the worst case in blocks (no fragmentation) helps a little; allocating on demand more than doubles the batch.
Requests finished in 4,000 steps, assuming every step takes the same time. On-demand allocation finishes about 2.1x more than paged reservation.
Preemptions. Both reserving policies never preempt. On demand preempted 420 times and had to recompute about 230,000 prompt tokens, a cost this simplified model does not charge.

blocks.md: Preemption is not free throughput. The optimistic policy's extra batch size is partly spent redoing prefills, and a preempted request's latency can jump by a full prefill plus queueing. Frequent preemption is a sign the pool is too small for the configured concurrency.

Admission control is a bet about future output lengths. Reserve the worst case and you never preempt but waste memory; allocate on demand and you fit far more requests but need a preemption policy (latest arrival first, all of its blocks) and a recovery method (swap or recompute).

blocks.question: A service promises customers that a started response will never stall mid-stream, even at the cost of throughput. Which TensorRT-LLM capacity policy fits?
options: MAX_UTILIZATION
STATIC_BATCH
GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT
Any of them, since in-flight batching never pauses requests
blocks.explain: GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT reserves the blocks each request needs to finish before starting it, so started requests are never paused. MAX_UTILIZATION trades that guarantee for more concurrency. STATIC_BATCH is a legacy mode the docs advise against for production.

blocks.question: Why does vLLM preempt the latest-arrived request rather than the one holding the most blocks?
options: The latest request always holds the fewest blocks, so it is cheapest
First come, first served: evicting latecomers protects older requests from repeated preemption and starvation
Older requests cannot be preempted because their blocks are shared
The CPU swap space only accepts recent blocks
blocks.explain: The paper adopts FCFS for fairness and to prevent starvation, so early arrivals are served first and the latest are preempted first. Evicting the biggest request would free more memory but could evict the same long request again and again.

blocks.question: Spot the bug: a scheduler allocates blocks on demand, admits a new request whenever its prompt's blocks are free, and has no preemption code. What eventually happens under heavy load?
options: Running requests need new blocks that are not there, so the step cannot proceed: an out-of-memory failure or a deadlock
Nothing, block allocation can never fail
Throughput drops but every request still finishes
Requests are silently truncated to their prompt length and returned
blocks.explain: On-demand allocation without a fallback is exactly the deadlock Orca's reservation avoids: every running request may need one more block at the same moment. You need either worst-case reservation or preemption with swap or recompute.

blocks.md: **vLLM.** The engine core's scheduler hands each request a share of a per-step token budget, with no hard split between prefill and decode, so chunked prefill, prefix caching and speculative decoding all fit one mechanism. Scheduling is FCFS by default, or by priority with FCFS as tie-breaker. `KVCacheManager` allocates from a `BlockPool` created at startup. When `allocate_slots` fails, the scheduler preempts the lowest-priority running request (the last one under FCFS), frees its blocks and puts it back in the waiting queue to be recomputed.

**SGLang.** Its source describes two levels of memory pool: `ReqToTokenPool` maps each request to its token locations, and a token-to-KV allocator manages indices into the physical KV cache. Freed KV stays in the `RadixCache` tree for reuse until evicted. Admission uses the estimated-future-tokens rule from the last lesson, and decode retraction handles overflow. Since v0.4 the scheduler runs one batch ahead (the team calls it a zero-overhead batch scheduler), hiding CPU work such as radix tree matching behind GPU compute.

**TensorRT-LLM.** The KV cache is a pool of blocks; tokens per block is a power of two, all layers of a token range share a block, and GQA models get blocks sized for their KV heads only. A `CapacityScheduler` (default policy `GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT`) reserves resources, then a `MicroBatchScheduler` builds the step's batch, prioritizing requests already generating. Filled blocks enter a radix search tree for reuse across requests, evicted by priority, then least recently used, and can be offloaded to secondary memory instead of dropped.

When tuning any of the three, find the same four numbers: KV pool size (gpu_memory_utilization or free_gpu_memory_fraction), max sequences per step (max_num_seqs or max_batch_size), max tokens per step (max_num_batched_tokens or max_num_tokens) and block size. Most performance surprises are one of these limits binding when you did not expect it.

blocks.prompt: Your vLLM logs keep warning that sequences are preempted in RECOMPUTE mode because there is not enough KV cache space, and p99 latency is bad. GPU compute is not saturated. What would you try first?
blocks.reveal: Give the KV cache more room or ask for less of it at once, as vLLM's docs suggest: raise `gpu_memory_utilization`, or lower `max_num_seqs` or `max_num_batched_tokens` so fewer sequences grow at the same time, or add tensor or pipeline parallelism to spread the weights. Each preemption throws away KV and redoes a prefill, so removing them often improves both tail latency and throughput.

blocks.md: Strip away names and every engine is the same loop: a scheduler spending a per-step token budget, a block allocator answering whether it fits, and a policy for when it does not. The engines differ mainly in that last policy and in how they reuse cached blocks.

blocks.question: Which statement about the three engines is accurate according to their documentation?
options: All three swap preempted KV caches to CPU memory by default
SGLang keeps every running request's full max_new_tokens reserved until it finishes
vLLM V1 runs prefill and decode in separate scheduler queues with separate budgets
TensorRT-LLM's default capacity policy never pauses a request once started, while vLLM V1 recomputes preempted requests
blocks.explain: GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT is TensorRT-LLM's default and guarantees started requests are not paused; vLLM V1 recomputes by default and removed CPU swapping for preemption. SGLang counts running requests' remaining tokens at an estimated ratio rather than their full maximum, and vLLM V1 uses one unified token budget.

blocks.question: A deployment serves a chat app where most requests share a long system prompt. Which component from the figure is responsible for turning that into saved prefill work?
options: The prefix cache index (hash table, radix tree or block-reuse tree)
The frontend process
The model executor
The capacity scheduler's no-evict policy
blocks.explain: The cache index finds blocks whose keys and values were already computed for the same prefix, so the new request's prefill skips those tokens. The PagedAttention and prefix caching course covers how vLLM's block hashes and SGLang's radix tree do this.
